texts.title: New Media and Social Movements
paras: Since the 1990s, there have been growing discussions of internet activism and how new media have been used effectively by a variety of political movements. The early adoption and successful use of the Internet in the early 1990s by the indigenous EZLN 1 Zapatista movement in the Chiapas region of Mexico quickly dramatized how new media and grass roots

progressivism might synergize, excite the world, and challenge status quo culture and politics. Activists who were already using the Internet as a technology for organizing and communicating in digital hubs, such as The Well quickly drew upon the Zapatista’s imaginative use of the Internet to begin broadcasting and tailoring their own messages to an emerging global audience.

According to Shirky (2011), the ability to spread messages without hierarchical coordination has frequently proven to be a powerful tool in impairing existing power structures and forcing political change. In 2001, Filipinos used text messages to coordinate a public protest of more than a million demonstrators in downtown Manila, which helped to ensure the impeachment of Philippine President Joseph Estrada. The same strategy was used in 2004 to force Spanish Prime Minister José María Aznar from office, and in 2009 the Communist Party lost power in Moldova after the protests coordinated by the same means. Thanks to social media, larger groups can now take on some kinds of coordinated action, such as protest movements and public media campaigns, which were previously reserved for formal organizations (Shirky, 2011).

While social media certainly provides benefits, it is not a guarantor of political change. Iran’s Green Movement in 2009 and the 2010 Red Shirt uprising in Thailand are examples of movements coordinated through social media that were ultimately eliminated by the violent crackdown of the governments being challenged. Shirky (2011) points out that when new media increases public access to speech or assembly, “a state accustomed to having a monopoly on public speech finds itself called to account for anomalies between its view of events and the public’s.” This new challenge of power is met with either censorship or physical force, and physical force is often the most desirable means of suppressing political activism.

Khondker (2012) highlights the challenge oppressive regimes now face when trying to crush social dissent. Globalization as a complex social, economic, and technological process can be viewed in terms of the spread and wider availability of communication technology, which improves connectivity. Such connectivity is as vital for facilitating business transactions as it is for social interactions and mobilizations. There is a fundamental contradiction in this process since it is often the government, aided by corporate interests, that promotes the new

movement media; thus, unintentionally creating a space for civic activism. This is why rapid, violent crackdown is often a more widely preferred means in many countries since censorship usually means shutting down Internet access or cell phone networks, which might harm the economy.

The Arab Spring uprisings, which began in December 2010, provide a valuable case study for the extent to which social media can force political change. While social media undoubtedly played a vital role in organizing political movements in countries throughout the Middle East, it is important to note that many were unsuccessful in achieving the political ends they sought. In the so-called Facebook or Twitter revolutions in Tunisia and Egypt, for example, social network sites and the Internet were useful tools, but conventional media played a crucial role in presenting the uprisings to the larger global community, who in turn supported the transformations. In addition to that, it took a military assistance that lasted eight months to collapse Muammar Gaddafi’s regime in Libya. The uprising in Bahrain—also fueled by the use of social media—was unsuccessful not only because it faced a violent government crackdown but also because those backups were absent.

It is certainly important not to fall into the trap of cyber-utopian thinking (Morozov, 2011), but the role social media now plays in triggering the rise of social movements and political activism cannot be discounted. In Tunisia and Egypt, revolutionary conditions such as government corruption, violent oppression, and economic imbalance laid the groundwork for the exploitation of new media by the people as a means of organizing. Connectivity was vital to spreading the message of revolution both before and during the dramatic demonstrations in Cairo’s Tahrir Square. As Khondker (2011) puts it, “social media was a vital tool—a necessary condition—especially in the face of a silenced conventional local media, but a tool nevertheless. It was not a sufficient condition.” This highlights the difficulty in critiquing the efficiency of social media as a force for political progress, or at least, political change. We cannot say with certainty whether or not those successful political movements in which social media played a central role could have succeeded without the technology. What seems apparent, however, is that it definitely did not hurt.

Those who criticize social media activism as “slacktivism3” (Gladwell, 2010) narrowly focus their critique on movements that never escape the virtual space. As Shirky (2011) points out, “the fact that some actors cannot move ahead to a better world does not mean that devoted actors cannot use social media effectively.” In Gladwell’s critique, he points out that the socalled “Twitter Revolution” inside Iran actually did not happen inside Iran. “The people tweeting about the demonstrations were almost all in the West”. Regardless of where the tweets were coming from, the mainstream media reported heavily on them, and the widespread press coverage increased international support for the movements, especially in the West, thus giving greater legitimacy to the movement in the global public sphere. And while the lack of a public sphere within Iran explains the ultimate defeat of the movement, it seems prudent to look more

of posting badges, images, apps, or text on social media without taking further action. broadly at the benefits of social media. As Shirky puts it, “The more promising way to think about social media is as long-term tools that can strengthen civil society and the public sphere.”

As Gladwell’s negative critique of social media suggests, it is simply a form of organizing which favors the weak-tie connections4 that give us access to information over the strong-tie connections5 that help us endure in the face of danger. Castells (2008) picks up where Gladwell seems to stop short. Castells asserts that the diffusion of Internet, mobile communication, digital media, and a variety of tools of social software have motivated the development of horizontal networks of interactive communicatio n that connect local and global in chosen time. Castells highlights the phenomenon of “mass self-communication,” which is “self-generated in content, self-directed in emission, and self-selected in reception by many that communicate with many.” It is through this new virtual space where global interaction by those who represent the force of “counter-power” is made possible. Counter-power is “the capacity of a social actor to resist and challenge power relations that are institutionalized” (Castells, 2008). Global capitalism, often referred to simply as globalism, is the dominant global institution through which hierarchies of power are determined, and communication technologies such as social media are vital to the maintenance of counter-power in this new global environment. These technologies make possible the unlimited diversity and the largely autonomous origin of most of the communication flows that construct, and reconstruct every second the global and local production of meaning in the public mind (Castells, 2008). In other words, “Access to information is far less important, politically, than access to conversation … As with the printing press, the Internet spreads not just media consumption but media production as well – it allows people to privately and publicly articulate and debate conflicting views” (Shirky, 2011).

If global capitalism stands as the supreme manifestation of sociopolitical power, it is important to analyze the effects of social media on multinational corporate interests. The online petition platform Change.org offers a fascinating case study for how individual opposition to private business practices is being channeled into widespread public opposition. The resultant public outcry creates a possible threat to the financial interests of these companies, causing them to surrender to the demands of the counter-power movement. Molly Katchpole is perhaps one of the best examples of the efficiency and future potential for online activism. In 2011, the 22-year-old nanny generated a petition on Change.org, criticizing Bank of America’s announcement of a new $5-a-month fee for debit cards. Katchpole’s petition got more than 306,000 signatures in a month, and after the petition attracted some mainstream national media coverage, Bank of America and other large financial institutions withdrew plans for the fee. Not long after, Katchpole started a second petition, protesting a $2 charge by Verizon, a major telecommunication provider, for online bill payments. It attracted more than 160,000 signatures in just 48 hours, and Verizon withdrew the fee (Kristof, 2012). Verizon had to reverse its plan but ironically, it is likely a safe assumption that Verizon managed to benefit from this negative publicity and increased its revenues. Sites such as Change.org provide empirical, quantitative data for measuring the efficiency of so-called “slacktivism” and its real-world effects on global

strong-tie connections: the interactions within communities and among people who have a lot of connections. capital markets. According to Change.org’s website, “There are more than 20 million Change.org users in 196 countries, and every day people use [their] tools to transform their communities – locally, nationally and globally”. In 2010, there were one million Change.org users. If the explosive growth of sites like Change.org is an accurate indicator of the potential for even greater impact in the future, then social activism in the virtual sphere is going to continue to be a strong force of counter-power.

The online petition is but one of the many examples of the effectiveness of viral communication in the digital age. On January 18, 2012, several popular websites employed the power of online social activism to spread their message of opposition to two bills that were making their way through Congress. The Stop Online Piracy Act and the Protect IP Act both heavily favored content providers in the entertainment industry, which played a large role in lobbying Congress to pass the legislation. The acts, according to several major players in the new media business, went too far in imposing broad restrictions on information flows within the digital realm. According to Jamar (2012), there was an uprising among innumerable Internet entrepreneurs and tech-savvy experts who analyzed the law and publicized the domestic damage it could do to them and to many other online businesses. The popular websites Wikipedia and Reddit led a strategic online communication campaign to raise awareness and fuel opposition to the bills, blacking out their sites for the day and encouraging their broad network of users to spread the message of opposition online and to contact their congressional representatives. Although it stopped short of completely shutting down its page for the day, Google also joined the black-out campaign. Ultimately, the broad, unquestioning support for the bills in Congress evaporated” (Jamar, 2012).

The examples above suggest that the new media has offered new means of communication as well as a wider arena for public to voice their concerns. It seems that the effectiveness of those tools will be evaluated better in the future but the current state is promising for more organized civil movements.

texts.title: Sugar and Society
paras: The use of sugar and sugar production dates back to ancient times. On the island of New Guinea, where sugar cane was domesticated some 10,000 years ago, people picked cane and ate it raw. Sugar spread from island to island in the south-western Pacific Ocean, finally reaching the Asian mainland around 1000 B.C. By A.D. 500 it was being processed into a powder in India and used for many things including the treatment of headaches and stomach problems. For many years, sugar refinement remained as a secret science, passed from master to his son. By A.D. 600 the art had spread to Persia, and then when Arab armies conquered the region, they carried away the knowledge and love of sugar, and turned the art into an industry. The work was still brutally difficult, however. By A.D. 1500, with the demand for sugar rising, the work was considered suitable only for the lowest of labourers.

The sugar that eventually reached the West was consumed only by the very wealthy as it was so rare. European soil and climate made it almost impossible to grow sugar cane. The European ‘Age of Exploration’, the search for new land that would send Europeans all around the world, was in reality a hunt for fields where sugar cane would prosper in the tropical temperatures and rainfall. In 1425 the Portuguese prince known as Henry the Navigator sent sugar cane to Madeira with an early group of colonists. The crop soon made its way to other newly discovered Atlantic islands. Then, in September 1493, when Christopher Columbus set off from Spain on his second voyage to the Americas, he too carried cane. Thus began the age of big sugar production in the Caribbean islands.

As more cane was planted, the price of the product fell, and as the price fell, demand increased. Economists call it a ‘virtuous cycle’. In the mid-17th century sugar began to change from a luxury spice to an essential part of the diet: first for the middle class, then for the poor. There was no stopping the boom. In 1700 the average Englishman consumed four pounds a year. Today the average American consumes 77 pounds of added sugar annually, or more than 22 teaspoons of added sugar a day.

‘It seems like every time I study an illness and trace a path to the first cause, I find my way back to sugar,’ says Richard Johnson, a nephrologist at the University of Colorado Denver. ‘Why is it that one-third of adults [worldwide] have high blood pressure, when in 1900 only 5% had high blood pressure?’ he asks. ‘Why did 153 million people have diabetes in 1980, and now we’re up to 347 million? Sugar, we believe, is one of the culprits, if not the major culprit.’ This is not a novel theory. In the 1960s the British nutrition expert John Yudkin conducted a series of experiments on animals and people showing that high amounts of sugar in the diet led to high levels of fat and insulin in the blood – risk factors for heart disease and diabetes. But Yudkin’s message was silenced by many other scientists blaming the rising rates of obesity and heart disease on cholesterol caused by too much saturated fat in the diet.

As a result, fat makes up a smaller portion of the American diet than it did 20 years ago. Yet the portion of America that is obese has only grown larger. The primary reason, says Johnson, along with other experts, is sugar, and in particular fructose. Sucrose, or table sugar, is composed of equal amounts of glucose and fructose, the latter being the kind of sugar you find naturally in fruit. It’s also what manufacturers use to give table sugar its sweetness, and which is found in large quantities in soft drinks and candy. Johnson summed up the conventional wisdom this way: Americans are obese because they eat too much and exercise too little. But they eat too much and exercise too little because they’re addicted to sugar, which not only makes them fatter but also reduces their energy.

The solution? Stop eating so much sugar. When people cut back, many of the ill effects disappear. The trouble is, in today’s world it’s extremely difficult to avoid sugar: manufacturers use sugar to hide the bad taste in foods that are low in fat, so they seem more healthful and taste better. But if sugar is so bad for us, why do we crave it? The short answer is that an injection of sugar into the bloodstream stimulates the pleasure centers of the brain. All tasty foods do this to some extent— but sugar has a sharply noticeable effect. In this sense it is literally addictive.

texts.title: The Dancing Mania
paras: Human history is full of bizarre occurrences, epidemics and interesting episodes. A rare phenomenon that first occurred in Europe in the Middle Ages and that was observed at intervals until the 17th century is the "Dancing mania", which is also known as the "dancing plague", "choreomania" and "St. Vitus dance". The dance involved groups of people, sometimes thousands at a time, who danced uncontrollably and bizarrely. The dancers would also scream, shout, and sing, and claim to have visions or hallucinations. The dancing mania affected men, women, and children, who danced until they collapsed from exhaustion. Generally, musicians accompanied dancers to keep off the mania, but this tactic sometimes backfired by encouraging more to join in.

The epidemic affected thousands of people across Europe, and outbreaks are reported in historical records. There is no consensus among modern-day scientists as to the cause of the dancing mania. Several theories proposed that people danced either to be a part of a religious cult or to relieve themselves of stress due to poverty. Some believe that dancing mania still lives on today in forms such as all-night parties, laughing epidemics, and other episodes of mass hysteria.

The earliest known outbreak of dancing mania occurred in the 7th century and it reappeared many times across Europe until about the 17th century, when it stopped abruptly. In the 13th century in central Germany, a group of children, more than a hundred actually, perhaps due to a psychological or neurological or physiological problem, travelled from Erfurt to Arnstadt - a distance of about 20 km-jumping and dancing all the way, in a marked similarity to the legend of the "Pied Piper of Hamelin". According to the account of an old chronicle, many of them, after they were taken home by their parents, died, and the rest remained affected to the end of their lives. Another incident in 1278 involved about 200 people dancing on a bridge over the River Mosel in Germany, resulting in its collapse. Many of the survivors were taken to the nearby church of St. Vitus for treatment. However, the first major outbreak of the mania occurred between 1373 and 1374, with incidents reported in Germany, England and the Netherlands. Then, it spread to France, Italy, and Switzerland. The largest episode was recorded in 1518, when a woman, Frau Toffea, began to dance in a street in Strasbourg. This lasted somewhere between four to six days. Within a week, 34 others had joined, and within a month, there were around 400 dancers. In all of these cases, some of the victims eventually died from heart attack, stroke, or exhaustion. Historical documents are clear that the victims danced, but it is not known why these people danced to their deaths.

Generally occurring in times of hardship, up to tens of thousands of people would appear to dance for hours, days, weeks, and even months. Females have often been pictured in modern literature as the usual participants in dancing mania, although contemporary sources suggest otherwise. Whether the dancing was spontaneous, or an organized event is also debated. What is certain, however, is that dancers seemed to be in a state of unconsciousness, and unable to control themselves.

In Italy, a similar phenomenon to dancing mania was "tarantism", in which the victims were said to have been poisoned by a tarantula or scorpion. The only antidote known was to dance to a particular music to separate the venom from the blood. Dancers would perform a tarantella, accompanied by music which eventually would cure the victim, at least temporarily. Some victims died if there was no music to accompany their dancing. Typically, those affected had similar symptoms to dancing mania, such as headaches, trembling, twitching, and visions. As with dancing mania women were reported to be most affected, but unlike dancing mania, tarantism was confined to Italy and southern Europe. It was a common phenomenon until the 17th century, but ended suddenly, with only very small outbreaks in Italy as late as 1959.

As the real cause of the dancing mania was unknown, many of the treatments for it were simply hopeful guesses, although some did seem effective. The 1374 outbreak occurred only decades after the Black Death, and was treated in a similar fashion: dancers were isolated and some were exorcised. People believed that St. Vitus was the patron saint of the victims of the dancing mania and they responded by praying and making pilgrimages to places dedicated to St. Vitus. Others claimed to be possessed by demons, or Satan; therefore, exorcisms were often performed on dancers. Often music and more dance too were used as remedies for the disease, and special places were set up for those afflicted to dance to the accompaniment of music.

Historian John Waller thinks that the dancing epidemic was caused by mass psychogenic illness (MPI), a form of mass hysteria that often follows extreme levels of psychological distress. Waller states that there are three causes of the MPI. Famine as the main cause had been prevalent in the region for some time, caused by very wet summers, crop frosts, and violent hailstorms. Those who survived were forced to kill their farm animals, take out loans, and perhaps even beg in the streets. In addition to famine, diseases such as smallpox afflicted the population, as well as a general feeling of hopelessness. All these three might have triggered the MPI.

Hecker, too, writes that regions around rivers Rhine and Maine had met with great catastrophes, floods destroyed everything people owned, "security of property there was none, arbitrary will everywhere prevailed; corruption of morals and rude power rarely met even with the weakest opposition". Hetherington and Munro describe dancing mania as a result of "shared stress". People may have danced to relieve themselves of the stress owing to the impoverishment of the day and in doing so attempted to become ecstatic and see visions. Sociologist Bartholomew contends that the dance was part of an "ecstatic ritual of heretical sect." These religious groups were making pilgrimages to parts of Europe, gathering followers as they went along. This explanation is questioned by Waller, who believes "there is no evidence that the dancers wanted to dance, citing recorded evidence that the dancers showed expressions of fear and desperation.

It has also been suggested that the cause of the dancing epidemic was ergotism, which results from consuming ergot-laced bread. Ingestion of ergot, a psychotropic mold (fungus) that grows on rye, can lead to delirium, hallucinations, and seizures, as well as other symptoms. During floods and damp periods, ergots were able to grow and affect rye and other crops. While today this is called ergotism, contemporaneously it was known as "Saint Anthony's fire". However, another symptom of ergotism is loss of blood supply to the limbs, making coordinated movement like dancing difficult, as such, Waller considers it to be an unlikely cause of the dancing mania. Hecker, too, states that ergotism can cause hallucinations like dancing mania does but cannot account for the other strange behavior most commonly identified with dancing mania. Bartholomew asserts that most epidemics of dancing did not coincide with flooding or wet growing or harvesting periods.

Some researchers claim the medieval dancing mania was in fact a chorea epidemic. Chorea can be present in epilepsy or a variety of other nervous system disorders. It is characterized by brief, irregular muscular contractions that are not repetitive or rhythmic, but appear to flow from one muscle to the next. The term Chorea Saint Viti was originally used for the dancing mania of the 15th and 16th centuries. The word "chorea" comes from the Greek word for dance. Paracelsus (14931541) described the symptoms and termed the disease chorea naturalis. Later Sydenham observed the disease in its weaker form – chorea minor.

Sydenham's chorea occurs in a small percentage (20 percent) of children and adolescents as a complication of rheumatic fever. The affected child in mild cases often appears restless. The jerky movements of the feet or hands are often similar to dancing or piano playing. When chorea is severe, the movements may cause motion of the arms or legs that results in tossing whatever is in the hand inadvertently or falling to the ground. Walking may become bizarre, with strange postures and leg movements. However, these do not justify how so many dancing mania cases could arise in the population, nor how so many adults were affected in the outbreaks. Besides, dancing mania had greatly declined in Sydenham's time, and it is unlikely that he himself observed the phenomenon.

texts.title: Understanding Social Movements
paras: Karl Marx, in the 1840s, famously pronounced, 'Philosophers have only interpreted the world in different ways; the point is to change it.' In many respects, this summarizes the essence of what social movements are about. Social movements are forms of collective action that emerge in response to situations of inequality, oppression, and/or unmet social, political, economic or cultural demands. In other words, they are collective forms of protest or activism that aim to affect some kind of transformation in existing structures of power that have created inequality, injustice, disadvantage, and so on. This does not mean that social movements are always positive or progressive. They can also be conservative, reactionary, or regressive.

Questions as to the efficacy of social movements lie at the heart of social movement studies. To what extent do movements like “Occupy” and the “Arab Spring” actually change things or make a difference? The upshot for those who hold a pessimistic view of society and radical politics is that there is no way to stand up against the current status quo. It is easy to see why they lack optimism or hope for any genuine alternative. However, while to these people, disengagement is the only option, others have become so enraged they feel there is no alternative other than to get involved in protests, demonstrations, marches, and the like. This proved to be the case with the Indignados in Spain1, Occupy, and the Arab Spring. Indeed, the recent global emergence of Occupy and the Arab Spring across the countries of the Middle East was seen as a beacon of hope for radical politics and democratic change in the contemporary period.

In order to understand social movements, it is of utmost importance to talk about collective behavior because social movements are one of the four primary forms of collective behavior along with the crowd, the mass, and the public.

The Indignados in Spain: anti-austerity (rigid economy) movement demanding radical change in Spanish politics. Started on May 15, 2011. line to get on the bus. Conventional crowds are those who come together for a scheduled event, like a theatre play or rock concert without acting out. Expressive crowds are people who join together to express emotion. They participate in crowd behavior by singing, dancing, screaming, shouting, cheering, clapping, or stomping their feet, lamenting, crying, mourning and so on as can be seen, for example, in a political rally for a candidate. People in the rally are there to support the candidate; and for this, they have to express themselves, for example, by shouting some slogans. The final type is acting crowds, people participating in protest movements or riots for example. They focus on a special goal or action, such as changing something they complain about. They are spontaneous and momentary lacking organization, leadership, identity and a 'we-consciousness'.

The Mass: A relatively large and dispersed number of people with a common interest whose members are largely unknown to one another and who are incapable of acting together in a concerted way to achieve objectives is called a mass. People who are excited by some national event, people who are interested in a murder trial, which is reported in the press, or people who participate in some large migration are all examples of masses. In this sense, the audience of the television show Game of Thrones or of any mass medium actually (TV, radio, films, books, newspapers) is a mass.

The Public: Blumer defines public as a group of people who, first are confronted by an issue, second are divided in their opinion as to how to address the issue, and third are engaged in discussion about the issue. A public is an unorganized, relatively diffused group of people who exchange ideas on an issue, which distinguishes it from a mass since the members of a mass hold the same interests without an opportunity to share ideas.

Social movements differ from other forms of collective behavior in that they aim to bring about or resist change in society. McCarthy and Zald (1977) define social movement as a 'set of opinions and beliefs in a population representing preferences for changing some element of the social structure or reward distribution dynamics'. A counter movement, on the other hand, refers to 'a set of opinions and beliefs in a population opposed to a social movement'. A simple example here might be the fight by anti-vivisectionists to stop experimentation on animals (a social movement), which is met with resistance from research scientists (a counter movement), claiming that animal vivisection2 is necessary to find cures for human diseases and lifethreatening illnesses.

What motivates people to become involved in collective action in the first place is of key concern to social movement scholars. Some believe that people are motivated by emotions such as anger, indignation, and a sense of injustice; others think people are driven by thinking strategically about how they might best achieve political goals collectively.

For social movements to arise, there must first exist certain political, economic, or other problems that prompt people to be dissatisfied enough to begin and join a social movement. These problems might include a faltering economy; a lack of political freedom; certain policies carried out by a government; or discrimination based on gender, race and ethnicity, or sexual orientation. Without such structural strain, people would not have any reason to protest, and social movements would not arise.

Whatever the problem, the dissatisfaction it generates leads to shared discontent (also called shared grievances) among some or most of the population. This discontent arises in part because people feel deprived relative to some other group or to some ideal state they have not reached. This feeling is called relative deprivation. James C. Davies and Ted Robert Gun popularized the importance of relative deprivation for social protest. When a deprived group perceives that social conditions are improving, wrote Davies, they become hopeful that their lives are getting better. But if these conditions stop improving, they become frustrated and more inclined to turn to protest, collective violence, and other social movement activity. Both Davies and Gun emphasized that people's feelings of being relatively deprived were more important for their involvement in collective behavior than their level of actual deprivation.

In their website occupywallst.org, the supporters of the movement define themselves as follows: 'Occupy Wall Street (OWS) is a people-powered movement that began on September 17, 2011 in Liberty Square in Manhattan's Financial District, and has spread to over 100 cities in the United States and actions in over 1,500 cities globally. OWS is fighting back against the corrosive power of major banks and multinational corporations over the democratic process, and the role of Wall Street in creating an economic collapse that has caused the greatest recession in generations. The movement is inspired by popular uprisings in Egypt and Tunisia, and aims to fight back against the richest 1% of people that are writing the rules of an unfair global economy that is foreclosing on our future.

The Canadian, anti-consumerist, pro-environment group/magazine Adbusters initiated the call for a protest. The main issues raised by Occupy Wall Street were social and economic inequality, greed, corruption and the influence of corporations on government—particularly from the financial services sector. To achieve their goals, the protesters acted on consensusbased decisions made in general assemblies which emphasized direct action rather than petitioning authorities to address problems. The protesters were forced out of Zuccotti Park on November 15, 2011. They turned their focus to occupying banks, corporate headquarters, board meetings, foreclosed homes, and college and university campuses.

From its inception, a principal characteristic of Occupy Wall Street has been its pluralistic nature. This characteristic was and continues to be central to the phenomenon's success, helping it spread rapidly across the USA, capturing public imagination. Now the protest is broken and it is doubtful if the movement attained its initial goals but it obviously gained worldwide recognition and raised awareness on the issues it had set out to challenge.

texts.title: Learned Helplessness
paras: Life requires that organisms continually adapt their behavior to the realities they encounter in the world about them. Adjustment consists of coping mechanisms that organisms use both to fit themselves to environmental circumstances and to change those circumstances to fit their needs. Yet, research by psychologists has shown that some organisms exposed to uncontrollable events acquire learned helplessness, which then impairs their adjustment to later events that are, in theory, controllable. Learned helplessness refers to a generalized expectancy that events are independent of one’s responses. Individuals characterized by learned helplessness believe that there is not a cause-and-effect relationship between their own actions and consequent events. Hence, they believe that active efforts to cope are useless.

In 1967, Seligman and his associates were doing a number of experiments with dogs to examine the relationship between fear conditioning and instrumental learning. They strapped the dogs into a harness so that they could not escape and gave them moderately painful, but not physically damaging, electric shocks. Nothing the dogs did could affect the onset, the offset, the duration, or the intensity of the shocks. The shocks were therefore uncontrollable from the perspective of the dogs. After this experience, these dogs as well as dogs who had not undergone the original harness studies were placed in a two-compartment shuttle box which consisted of two sides. What they discovered was a distinct difference between the dogs who had originally been harnessed and those who had not. For the latter, when a shock was presented, they almost immediately, after trying different methods of escape, jumped across the barrier that separated the compartments to the safe, no-shock side. After a few trials, these dogs learned to jump as soon as the shock began, thereby significantly limiting the amount of shock they experienced at any given trial. The previously

harnessed dogs, on the other hand, showed a markedly different pattern of responses to the shock. Although at first they would run about the compartment and howl, they soon settled down and passively took the shock, whining quietly. The same pattern of behavior occurred in the following trials.

The researchers concluded that the experience in the harness had taught the dogs that their responses did not matter, and thus, they simply gave up. Much to their surprise, Seligman and his associates realized that they had come across a new phenomenon, which they named “learned helplessness.” In the following years, Seligman and various other researchers such as Maier (1970) and Peterson (1981) did further experiments both with other animals and human beings to test this new phenomenon.

One of these researchers, Donald Hiroto (1974), undertook a learned helplessness experiment with a sample of college students. The students were assigned to one of three groups: A, B and C. In the first phase of the experiment, Group A heard a loud noise that they could stop by pushing a button four times. Group B heard the noise, but could not escape from it. Group C did not receive any noise. In the second phase of the experiment, all the groups were tested with a “noise box” in which the subjects could turn off the sound simply by moving a lever from one side of the box to the other. The results were strikingly similar to those of the dog experiments, with students in one of the groups listening passively to the disturbing noise.

Educational psychologists find that children who give up when they confront failure in achievement situations are also victims of learned helplessness. Their motivational deficit in learning situations arises from the expectation that outcomes are uncontrollable. This perceived inability to overcome failure leads to uncaring attitude. Likewise, learned helplessness may find expression in social situations when children believe they cannot overcome rejection. Children who emphasize their personal incompetence as the source of their rejection are less likely than other children to pursue approval from their peers (Goetz and Dweck, 1980).

In a study undertaken by Carol S. Dweck and Dickon Reppucci (1973) in a school setting, one teacher gave solvable problems and another gave unsolvable problems to fifth-graders. When the “unsolvable-problem” teacher later presented solvable problems, some children did not solve them despite the fact that the problems were of the same sort as the ones they had solved for the oth er teacher. The researchers were able to compare those children who gave up in the face of failure with those who persevered. They found that the students that easily gave up took less personal responsibility for their successes and failures; they ascribed success and failure to ability rather than to effort.

In another study involving learned helplessness, Carol I. Diener and Dweck (1975) found a striking difference between “helpless” and “mastery-oriented” children in their approach toward failure. Helpless children tend to think about the cause of their lack of success. However, since they attribute failure to uncontrollable factors, they spend little time searching for ways to overcome failure. In contrast, mastery-oriented pupils appear to be less concerned with the causes of past errors and more concerned with finding a solution for the problem that confronts them. Other research reveals that helpless children underestimate their number of successes and overestimate their number of failures. Nor do helpless children, in contrast with mastery-oriented children, expect that they will continue to succeed (Diener and Dweck, 1980).

Dweck (1978) designed an experimental study to explore the effect of training on learned helplessness. The experimental group consisted of children who had had various experiences of failure, and had learned to be helpless. The other group included children with various success and some failure experiences. The students in the first group received training, whereas those in the latter group did not. Dweck successfully trained children characterized by learned helplessness to attribute their failure to a lack of effort rather than to a lack of ability. The children who were taught to make attributions that stressed motivation rather than ability as determinants of failure showed striking improvement in their coping responses to failure. However, the other group of helpless children, who were provided only with success experiences, continued to display difficulty when confronted with failure situations.

There has also been research into the gender differences in learned helplessness. A growing body of research suggests that girls are more likely to show evidence of learned helplessness than boys. For example, girls are more apt than boys to attribute failure to uncontrollable factors like lack of ability and to decrease their efforts following failure (Dweck and Repucci, 1973; Dweck and Gilliard, 1975; Nicholls, 1975). This occurs despite the fact that, on school-related tasks, girls are at least as proficient as boys. Indeed, girls receive consistently higher grades than boys and are more positively rated by teachers and other adults on most attributes.

Why do girls so readily put the blame on their abilities when confronted with failure despite the fact that the feedback they receive from their academic and social achievements always tells them they are highly regarded? Why do boys display greater confidence and persistence despite the fact that they receive more negative evaluations? Carol S. Dweck and her associates sought answers to these questions in classroom observations and experimental settings. Their research suggests that the pattern of evaluative feedback which teachers provide boys and girls with differs (1976, 1978).

Teachers tend to be much more critical of boys than girls. This, says Dweck, allows boys to attribute negative feedback to a characteristic of the teacher and not to themselves. Moreover, much of the negative evaluation that boys receive for their work is unrelated to its intellectual quality and is based instead upon neatness and following instructions. Accordingly, boys can view negative feedback as unrelated to the intellectual adequacy of their work. Finally, teachers attribute boys’ failures to lack of motivation. In contrast, teachers use negative feedback in a highly specific manner for girls’ intellectual failures; for boys, less than one-third of the negative evaluation is dependent upon the intellectual aspects of their work, whereas it is two-thirds for girls.

After stirring enormous interest among experimental psychologists for a decade, the concept of learned helplessness and the related experiments with dogs started to raise questions. Seligman claimed that both individuals who have developed learned helplessness and those with all sorts of depressive disorders manifested almost the same patterns of behavior. Depressed patients interpret their responses as either failing or doomed to failure. It is as if the depressed person is locked within a mental set that repeatedly registers, “I am a born loser.” However, critics pointed out that there are a great many different types of depressive disorders, each evidencing somewhat different symptoms (Depue and Monroe, 1978). In recognition of this fact, Seligman (1978) narrowed his interpretation to cover only a very limited subclass of depressions.

Another major problem with the theory, as John Teasdale of Oxford pointed out, was that the helplessness training procedure that had been used to demonstrate the validity of the theory seemed to work on two out of three subjects in each learned helplessness study. In other words, a third of the subjects resisted the training procedure, and showed no inclination towards becoming helpless. This observation, together with doubts expressed by two of his own graduate students, led Seligman, together with his critics, to recast the theory in more cognitive terms (Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale, 1978).

The reformulated theory of learned helplessness drew upon some of the ideas of Bernard Weiner of the University of California at Los Angeles. Weiner had been studying people’s explanatory styles (attributions) in achievement situations. He had found that whether people are inclined to persist or not persist at a task in the face of failure is linked, for example, to whether or not they concluded that the failure they were presently experiencing was simply a lack of effort on their part, or was due to something over which they had no control. The reformulated theory of learned helplessness expanded these ideas to help explain why some people become depressed and others never do (Abramson, Seligman and Teasdale, 1978; Miller and Norman, 1979).

This new theory suggests that the way people explain the reasons for the bad and good events that they experience is the main reason why some people become helpless, while some others do not, as a result of experiencing bad events (Peterson and Seligman, 1984). People who give up and become helpless believe that the causes of the unfortunate events that happen to them are permanent. People who do not give up, in contrast, believe that bad events are temporary. Failure tends to make almost everyone momentarily helpless. The people who succeed, however, are those who pick themselves up and try again.

On the other hand, later research into this reworking of the theory showed that both the hopeless self-blamer and the hopeful self-helper see that their behavior and emotions stem from internal factors. To deal with these difficulties, Abramson, Metalsky and Alloy (1989) modified the helplessness theory into a still broader the “hopelessness” theory. The hopelessness theory contends that, prior to becoming hopeless, the person has a negative cognitive style, or attribution style, and some unfortunate, stressful experience. Because both of these factors are involved, some people prone to depressive thinking do not become depressed since they develop the tendency to avoid traumatic experiences.

texts.title: Artificial Intelligence
paras: For centuries, if not millennia, humanity has concerned itself in fiction and often in engineering with the creation of devices designed to mimic human behavior, or to behave in a seemingly intelligent way. Even before science fiction brought the ideas of superhuman robots and megalomaniacal computers, people had built bowing statues, letter-writing dolls, and player pianos1 in an effort to make inanimate objects seem somehow more human or intelligent.

Like many technological advances of this century, the development of computer science began as a military effort during the war. In the early 1940s, both Germany and the United States were racing to produce electronic computers that could be used in ballistic calculations, or in deciphering coded messages. It was only after the World War II that computing facilities, often several rooms in size, could be spared for less essential tasks. The excess computing power after the war, coupled with some major advances in the design of the machines, provided a fertile ground for exploring some more unusual and untested ideas for computing.

Among the first researchers to attempt to build intelligent programs were Newell and Simon. Their first well-known program, Logic Theorist, was a program that proved (or attempted to prove) statements using the accepted rules of logic and a problem-solving program of their own design. Their results were promising: not only could Logic Theorist reproduce many of the proofs that humans had developed, but in the case of one theorem, it actually produced a superior (i.e. shorter, more direct) proof than the one commonly found in logic textbooks.

Hubert Dreyfus, a prominent critic of AI movement, notes that almost all early work in AI was concerned with one of the three areas: Language Translation, Problem Solving, or Pattern Recognition. In each area, significant early successes were produced. Language translation was an early leader: Dreyfus estimates that in the first 10 years of research program (that is between 1955 - 1965), five governments spent over $20 million on its development. By the late fifties, programs existed that could do a satisfactory job of translating technical documents and it was predicted that adding extra databases and more computing power would be enough for the program to be effective in less formal, more ambiguous texts. In reality, despite the additions of these two factors, the programs simply could not scale up in the predicted ways.

One fundamental reason why these programs did not work in anything other than clear and technical texts was the inability to use context in order to interpret the meanings of unclear words and sentences. In essence, this skill which exists naturally in humans was not present in the translation programs. By the mid-sixties, the program had been substantially scaled down. Although current research in this area has produced recent success, it is still considered one of the great failures of early AI, one of the first signs of over-optimism.

The last of the three early areas of AI was pattern recognition. Once again, there were some early successes. Computers were built to handle Morse code, if there was very little line noise, and the sender was another computer or a very efficient and precise human operator. There were even programs that could, with a reasonable (though not human level) degree of accuracy decipher handwriting (or at least, the letter "A") in various styles. None, however, did so by way of some fundamental discovery in pattern recognition. Instead, they used ultra-specific and inflexible patterns, and they simply did not work when there was any distortion or uncertainty in the data. They were incapable of resolving ambiguity by utilizing context.

The initial successes of computers in replicating seemingly intelligent behavior quickly led to argument and speculation about what it would mean for a computer to be 'intelligent'. As any psychology student knows, intelligence is a very controversial topic, which makes the classification of a man-made machine as intelligent even harder. In terms of raw calculation power, even computers of the mid 1950s could beat human counterparts. The brute force calculations of programs like Newell and Simon's Logic Theorist had already produced results that, if a human had produced them, he would be definitely accepted as intelligent. Still the debate raged on. The argument focused on the fact that there was no ingenuity, no perception, and the computer merely followed human-programmed rules mindlessly until it reached a conclusion.

The developers of AI were claiming more than just replication of intelligent products, though. They claimed the replication of the intelligence process (this was later referred to by Searle as the Strong AI position). In other words, they were beginning to claim not only that computers were intelligent, but that they were intelligent in the same way as people are intelligent. Suddenly the debate became more than just a philosophical one, psychology entered the picture. If intelligent computers were produced, could they be considered a working model of human intelligence? All the computers to date, systems like the GPS were mindless rule-followers, what did that say about human intelligence? If we accept them as intelligent, does it necessarily follow that they must be intelligent in the way we are? These were significant questions for psychologists and philosophers, as well as computer scientists. The Turing Test

Alan Turing, in a 1951 paper, proposed a test called "The Imitation Game" that might finally settle the issue of machine intelligence. The first version of the game involved no computer intelligence whatsoever. Imagine three rooms, each connected via computer screen and keyboard to the others. In one room sits a man, in the second a woman, and in the third sits a person – let’s call him or her the "judge." The judge's job is to decide which of the two people talking to him through the computer is the man. The man will attempt to help the judge, offering whatever evidence he can (the computer terminals are used so that no physical clues can be used) to prove his man-hood. The woman's job is to deceive the judge so she will attempt to deceive him and counteract her opponent's claims, in hopes that the judge will erroneously identify her as the male.

What does any of this have to do with machine intelligence? Turing then proposed a modification of the game, in which instead of a man and a woman as contestants, there was a human, of either gender, or a computer at the other terminal. Now the judge's job is to decide which of the contestants is human, and which is the machine. Turing proposed that if, under these conditions, a judge were less than 50% accurate, that is, if a judge is as likely to pick either human or computer, then the computer must be a passable simulation of a human being and hence, intelligent.

Partly out of an attempt to pass Turing's test, and partly just for the fun of it, there arose, largely in the 1970s, a group of programs that tried to cross the first human-computer barrier: language. These programs, often fairly simple in design, employed small databases of (usually English) language combined with a series of rules for forming intelligent sentences. While most were inadequate, some grew to tremendous popularity. Perhaps the most famous such program was Weizenbaum's ELIZA. Written in 1966 it was one of the first and remained for quite a while one of the most convincing. ELIZA simulates a Rogerian psychotherapist (the Rogerian therapist is emphatic, but passive, asking leading questions but doing very little talking, eg. "Tell me more about that," or "How does that make you feel?") and does so quite convincingly, for a while. There is no hint of intelligence in ELIZA's code, it simply scans for keywords like "Mother" or "Depressed" and then asks suitable questions from a large database. Failing that, it generates something broad in an attempt to elicit further conversation. Most programs since have relied on similar principles of keyword matching, paired with basic knowledge of sentence structure.

Although Turing proposed his test in 1951, it was not until 40 years later, in 1991, that the test was first really implemented. Dr Hugh Loebner, a professor very much interested in seeing AI succeed, pledged $100,000 to the first entrant that could pass the test. The 1991 contest had some serious problems though, (perhaps the most notable was that the judges were all computer specialists, and knew exactly what kind of questions might trick up a computer) and it was not until 1995 that the contest was re-opened. Since then there has been an annual competition, which has yet to find a winner. While small prizes have been given, no program has had the 50% success Turing aimed for. The Thought Experiment (an adaptation of Searle's original)

Searle asks the reader to imagine a room, with a man trapped inside. The man speaks no Chinese, nor could he even confidently distinguish Chinese characters from random lines of similar structure. One day, as he is sitting in the room, someone slips a piece of paper under the door with (what he assumes to be) Chinese writing on it. Having puzzled over it a bit, he notices that there is a book in the room titled "What to do if someone slides some Chinese writing under the door. Having nothing better to do, the man proceeds to open the book and begin reading. The book, he finds, is actually an enormous set of instructions for producing new Chinese symbols based on what comes in. The rules instruct him on how to produce new Chinese symbols, based on the ones received. They are all if-then type statements describing a pattern in the text and the appropriate action or response. He follows these rules, using the piece of paper handed to him, and he produces a new sheet, which he slides back under the door. The next day, another sheet comes in, he again opens the rule book, finds out which symbols to write and in which order, and passes the completed sheet back out. At no time does the man understand what he's doing as anything more than symbol manipulation, he does not understand the words coming in, or the words going out, he isn't even sure they ARE words but it's more exciting than doing nothing, so he continues. What the man in the room does not know, is that the symbols coming in are questions, written in Chinese, and that the symbols he produces in turn are answers to those questions. What's more, the book of instructions has been written so well that his answers are not only proper Chinese, but they make sense, and are indistinguishable from an actual Chinese speaker. Outside, the world is amazed that this room can actually understand Chinese, that the room is intelligent. Inside though, we know that the man understands no Chinese whatsoever!

Historically, human creativity has been a neglected topic in psychology in general and intelligence testing in particular. Despite this, creativity is considered by most to be an essential component of human intelligence. Consequently, in attempting to answer the question of whether computers can think, it is only natural to ask whether computers can think creatively. Many feel, in fact, that whereas computers can excel in well-structured areas of problem solving, e.g. logic, algebra, etc., they have little hope of producing truly creative work. For a work to be creative, it must be novel and useful, and this represents an enormous challenge for AI.

Another question related to AI is if computers can possess emotional intelligence. The rationale for attempting to mimic emotional intelligence in computer is not immediately clear. In fact, classic Western views of intelligence often pitted emotion and reason against each other. Emotion was seen as a disorganizing factor, harmful to reasoning and logic. However, with recent introduction of the concept of emotional intelligence, the many positive contributions of emotional factors to intellectual functioning have been recognized and highlighted. Furthermore, understanding emotion (and/or exhibiting it) may prove essential to any system that is designed to interact with human beings. Of course, the implementation of such a system represents an enormous challenge.

So why is understanding emotions crucial? The most direct reason and the obvious one - after a moment's examination - is that emotion is inextricably tied to everything we say and do. In more concrete terms, let us consider the advantages of having a computer that understood emotion. First of all, it could provide vastly improved interactions with users. More importantly, though, emotional intelligence would be a huge leap forward for systems attempting to learn about people, and the world in which they live.

texts.title: Changes in Reading Habits
paras: Look around on your next plane trip. The iPad is the new pacifier for babies and toddlers. Younger school-aged children read stories on smartphones; older kids don’t read at all, but hunch over video games. Parents and other passengers read on tablets or skim a flotilla of email and news feeds. Unbeknown to most of us, an invisible, gamechanging transformation links everyone in this picture: the neuronal circuit that underlies the brain’s ability to read is subtly, rapidly changing and this has implications for everyone from the pre-reading toddler to the expert adult.

As work in neurosciences indicates, the acquisition of literacy necessitated a new circuit in our species’ brain more than 6,000 years ago. That circuit evolved from a very simple mechanism for decoding basic information, like the number of goats in one’s herd, to the present, highly elaborated reading brain. My research depicts how the present reading brain enables the development of some of our most important intellectual and affective processes: internalized knowledge, analogical reasoning, and inference; perspective-taking and empathy; critical analysis and the generation of insight. Research surfacing in many parts of the world now cautions that each of these essential ‘deep reading’ processes may be under threat as we move into digital-based modes of reading.

This is not a simple, binary issue of print versus digital reading and technological innovations. As MIT scholar Sherry Turkle has written, we do not err as a society when we innovate but when we ignore what we disrupt or diminish while innovating. In this hinge moment between print and digital cultures, society needs to confront what is diminishing in the expert reading circuit, what our children and older students are not developing, and what we can do about it.

We know from research that the reading circuit is not given to human beings through a genetic blueprint like vision or language; it needs an environment to develop. Further, it will adapt to that environment’s requirements – from different writing systems to the characteristics of whatever medium is used. If the dominant medium advantages processes that are fast, multi-task oriented and well-suited for large volumes of information, like the current digital medium, so will the reading circuit. As UCLA psychologist Patricia Greenfield writes, the result is that less attention and time will be allocated to slower, time-demanding deep reading processes.

Increasing reports from educators and from researchers in psychology and the humanities bear this out. English literature scholar and teacher Mark Edmundson describes how many college students actively avoid the classic literature of the 19th and 20th centuries in favour of something simpler as they no longer have the patience to read longer, denser, more difficult texts. We should be less concerned with students’ ‘cognitive impatience’, however, than by what may underlie it: the potential inability of large numbers of students to read with a level of critical analysis sufficient to comprehend the complexity of thought and argument found in more demanding texts.

texts.title: Educating Psyche
paras: Educating Psyche by Bernie Neville is a book which looks at radical new approaches to learning, describing the effects of emotion, imagination and the unconscious on learning. One of the many theories discussed in the book is the one proposed by George Lozanov, which focuses on the power of suggestion.

Lozanov's instructional technique is based on the evidence that the connections made in the brain through unconscious processing (which he calls non-specific mental reactivity) are more durable than those made through conscious processing. Besides the laboratory evidence for this, we know from our experience that we often remember what we have perceived peripherally, long after we have forgotten what we actually tried to learn. If we think of a book we studied months or years ago, we will find it easier to recall peripheral details - the colour, the binding, the typeface, the table at the library where we sat while studying it - than the content on which we were concentrating. If we think of a lecture we listened to with great concentration, we will recall the lecturer's appearance and mannerisms, our place in the auditorium, the failure of the airconditioning, much more easily than the ideas we went to learn. Even if these peripheral details are a bit elusive, they come back readily in hypnosis or when we relive the event imaginatively, as in psychodrama. The details of the content of the lecture, on the other hand, seem to have gone forever.

This phenomenon can be partly attributed to the common counterproductive approach to study (making extreme efforts to memorise, tensing muscles, inducing fatigue), but it also simply reflects the way the brain functions. Lozanov therefore made indirect instruction (suggestion) central to his teaching system. In suggestopedia, as he called his method, consciousness is shifted away from the curriculum to focus on something peripheral. The curriculum then becomes peripheral and is dealt with by the reserve capacity of the brain.

texts.title: Business Ethics
paras: Ethics is the study of what is good and evil, right and wrong, and just and unjust. Business ethics, therefore, is the study of good and evil, right and wrong, and just and unjust actions in business. In general, ethical traditions that apply to business favor truth telling, honesty, protection of human and animal lives and rights, respect for the law, and adherence to socially accepted policies. Some of these touchstones go back thousands of years, whereas other ethical standards have emerged only recently.

Ethical managers try to do good and avoid doing evil following a mass of principles, values, norms and thoughts concerned with what conduct is right. However, the outlines of good and evil are indistinct; some ethical issues are hidden and hard to recognize, and some are very subtle and submerged in everyday workplace behavior. Therefore, the application of ethics in business is an art, an art which requires good judgment about both the motivations behind and the consequences of an act. There are two basic views trying to guide managers who have to make difficult ethical decisions.

The first theory, “the theory of amorality”, holds that business should be amoral, that is, conducted without reference to the full range of society’s ethical ideals. This view reached the peak of its popularity during the latter half of the nineteenth century, when it was widely believed that business and personal ethics existed in separate compartments, and that less idealistic ethics were permissible in business. The proponents of the theory claim that the market mechanism works in such a way that, by pursuing his or her own interest, a merchant frequently promotes that of the society more effectively than when he or she really intends to promote it. Although “the theory of amorality” now has far less public acceptance than it had in the past, it quietly lives on for many managers because it continues to release these managers from a burden of guilt that they might otherwise feel.

The second basic ethical orientation, “the theory of moral unity,” holds that business ethics cannot be based on a special set of more permissive rules than those of society. In other words, the demands of business life have to harmonize with basic ethics. Although selfish economic transactions may eventually be beneficial for society, profit-making should not be the only or the highest standard.

Ethical practice in business differs among countries and regions of the world because of the way environmental factors shape ethical values. One of these factors is historical experience, a broad factor that can shape ethical environments for business that are radically different. Russia had a long history of autocratic, oppressive rule lasting for centuries under the Orthodox Church and the monarchy, and ended the previous century with communist rule. This history of oppression led to the development of dual ethical standards for personal and business dealings. High ethical standards were always important in dealing with friends and family, but, through the centuries, deception and conspiracy in dealing with tyrannical officials in business life became permissible.

Under communism, party officials planned business activity in intricate detail, passing hundreds of thousands of laws, rules, and orders affecting every industry. Because it was impossible to comply with all these rules and be efficient in business, Soviet managers routinely broke rules, manipulated production data, and fabricated accounts to accomplish business goals. With the downfall of the Soviet regime, an entrepreneurial, free enterprise system started to grow in Russia alongside state-owned enterprises, but the ethics of this new business system are of a low standard.

Unlike in developed economies, unethical behavior and corruption may be inescapable in countries where the market economy is not supported by the institutions and traditions operating in those countries. This is the case in contemporary Russia, where many activities that are critical for free enterprise are illegal or unprotected by law. For instance, "speculation" or profit making, was a criminal offense in the Soviet Union and is now a gray area. The legislation is inherently weak in terms of regulating bankruptcy or mergers¹, contract disputes, and other important business activities. Even worse, an independent justice system does not exist to settle conflicts among business holders. In short, although communism is over, the shortcomings it created still continue to pose an obstacle to free enterprise.

In many underdeveloped and impoverished countries, the structure of civil institutions also fails to support high ethical standards. In these countries, businesses must fight to survive, and they see high ethics as an unaffordable luxury. In addition, some of these countries might lack democratic institutions that reinforce ethical standards. In this situation, consumers, workers, and others injured by unethical business conduct have neither the opportunity nor the experience to work through groups and governments for better behavior. However, in more advanced industrialized countries, established public values and regulatory bodies demand consistent ethical market behavior and punish wrongdoing harshly. This is a basic difference in the ethical climate and one that cannot be underestimated in its impact on managerial virtue.

The nature of the political system is another important factor. In European social democracies such as England, France, and the Netherlands, where governments have traditionally taken responsibility for alleviating social problems, corporations have had comparatively less voluntary discretion than American firms have. European companies are less likely to think in terms of ethical standards that are independent of government legal requirements. One reflection of this is that they are much less likely than U.S. companies to have formal, written ethics codes.

In developing countries, where the government is highly bureaucratic, the great number of rules and restrictions makes even simplest tasks so difficult that many have to resort to bribery, corruption, and personal favoritism. Friends are given favors in preference to strangers. Furthermore, to make sure they will receive payoffs², government officials in such countries have been known to paralyze business activity by strict application of innumerable laws. In the end, honest businesses either go bankrupt or get caught in the web of a system where unethical business conduct is inevitable. Philosophy and Religion The Case of the Far East versus the United States

Finally, philosophy and religion may have a deep impact on ethical values. Asian countries are deeply influenced by schools of thought that originated in ancient China. Asian managers who are inclined towards philosophy generally study Bing Fa, a form of strategic thinking developed in Chinese military doctrine beginning around 70 B.C. Bing Fa is based on the study of warfare. Since most Asians believe that all parts of human existence are interconnected and that universal principles discovered in one area can be applied in all areas of life, for Asian managers, the conduct of business resembles warfare. As a result of this, they think that a greater range of tactics are acceptable in business compared to their Western counterparts. For example, the Chinese, the Japanese, and Koreans may directly pry into trade secrets and secretly gather information about their competitors, or they may violate patent laws, partly because they consider that manipulations in the marketplace are justified by the lessons of Bing Fa.

One remarkable variation in business ethics arises from the emphasis on individualism in American culture as opposed to the emphasis on groups in many other cultures. Individualism in American social philosophy makes individual conscience the source of ethical control, which therefore makes personal guilt the penalty for bad conduct. However, in other countries, a combination of the underlying factors discussed above has created far different ethical values. The Japanese, for instance, have a strong ethic of fidelity to work groups and corporations. Beginning in about the sixth century, Japan, like other Asian societies, began to borrow and adapt Chinese culture. Traditional values in China stressed that an individual's primary obligation was not to the self but to others, including family, clan, and government. In Japan, recalcitrant individuals are avoided, as people are expected to work together well and towards the same goal. Most Japanese people prefer to work with compliant colleagues. Furthermore, the Japanese are not controlled by their guilty consciences. Rather, they are subjected to group disapproval.

The Confucian ethic of obedient loyalty is prominent in other Asian economies and creates some surprising results. There are many studies focusing on the effect of Confucian ethic and its implications on business. For example, a comparison study showed that older managers in Hong Kong more readily agreed to unethical practices than younger managers, just the reverse of the typical U.S. situation. Younger managers, under the influence of Eastern culture, are more tightly restricted in their behavior by work-group norms than are older managers, who have more independence to depart from rigid integrity.

texts.title: Attitudes Toward Business
paras: The list of specific criticisms of corporations is virtually endless, but they are all based on the same idea, which is that people in business value profit rather than important virtues such as honesty, truth, justice, love, respect for nature and so forth. For example, two critics, Jacobson and Mazur (1995), argue that commercialism has degraded the meaning of Christmas, by turning “the day commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ into a consumption mania.” In this instance, divinity is sacrificed for monetary gain, and, according to critics, the profit motive is less noble than humanitarian motives because it is seen as selfish.

In addition to the critics of business, a large number of people in many countries throughout the world share similar ideas. People believe that business cheats and harms consumers, exploits and dehumanizes workers, degrades nature and the environment, manipulates government and undermines public interest. For instance, opinion polls show that people may blame business for their economic troubles and in 1994 only 26 percent of Americans expressed a great deal of confidence in big businesses. At the root of these general ideas are attitudes toward business that have developed since ancient civilizations.

Throughout recorded history, people in most cultures have questioned the activities of merchants1 and businesses. The earliest societies, such as ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, the Inca and Aztec societies, old China, and the ancient Hindu kingdoms of Southeast Asia, were agrarian societies. An agrarian society is a pre-industrial society in which economic activity, government, and culture are based on traditions arising from agriculture. Upper social classes were comprised of wealthy landowners. No industry or mass-consumer markets existed, so business practice was only a tiny part of these ancient economies. In this setting, the sharp trading practices of merchants were often viewed as clashing with the traditional values of family and clan relations among farmers. Merchants typically had lower social status than government officials, farmers, soldiers, artisans, and teachers.

Both Greece and Rome were also based on subsistence agriculture, and economic activity of merchants, bankers, and manufacturers was limited. The largest factory in Athens, for example, employed 120 workers. Commercial activity was greater in Rome, but it was still fundamentally an agrarian society. Merchants in both societies achieved middle-class status below an upper class of landed aristocrats. However, because industrial activity was so limited in Greek civilization, no accurate and clear economic doctrines were developed to explain or justify commercial activity. In this environment, some great philosophers emphasized the idea that wealth, particularly wealth from commercial activity, was caused by greed.

Greed was regarded as particularly suspect in the limited economy of ancient Greece because the popular idea was that the amount of wealth was fixed. If so, an individual trying to increase wealth could only do it as long as the share of others was diminished. This created the idea that material acquisitiveness is not as noble and honorable as the desire for knowledge. The latter does not create social injustice; the former may.

These views were reflected first in Greek, and later in Roman culture. In the utopian society described in “The Republic”, for example, Plato prohibited the possession of private property by its rulers for fear of corruption and the rise of tyrants; they were forbidden even to touch gold or silver.

Later, Roman law would forbid the senatorial class to make business investments (although the law would be widely disobeyed by people). Likewise, the Stoic philosophers of Rome taught that, rather than owning property, the truly affluent person possessed inner peace. These thinkers looked down on merchants of their day as materialists who wasted their lives for wealth. Needless to say, this did not deter the merchants from accumulating fortunes.

During the Middle Ages, the prevalent theological doctrines of the Roman Catholic Church were intolerant against most commercial activities, such as profit making, market pricing and lending money for interest. Christianity created a doctrine against the values of the wealthy ruling class. It rejected a focus on wealth accumulation. The Church claimed that commerce deviated merchants from religion. Merchants were advised to put a fair price for their products. By the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, however, the money supply, as well as economic activity, expanded greatly. Commercial activity was stronger than fear of prison or hell. Like the ancient philosophical doctrines, the doctrines of The Medieval Church could not stop merchants from accumulating wealth. Even some church scholars such as St. Thomas Aquinas began to soften the doctrines that were against market pricing and profit making. Nonetheless, the lending of money for interest, the only business practice that The Roman Church had particularly condemned, was never embraced by The Church.

Unlike in most other countries, much higher levels of public confidence in business existed during the early years of the United States than now. Historians record generally positive feelings toward entrepreneurs, companies and business system. This might be because the commercial spirit was dominant in colonial America. For example, the farmer was not a peasant dependent on the soil. Although his way of life was different from the merchant in the town, they both engaged in buying and selling. As the farmers accumulated wealth, they used their money exactly like merchants. In contrast to those in Europe, American merchants who had great wealth rose to top status in colonial society because of the absence of hereditary aristocracy.
